# AFS-based inference of $N_e$

**Imagine you sequenced 1 Mb of sequence of ten individuals from a population
of your interest and computed a summary statistic such as the allele frequency
spectrum (AFS). Those sequences (and, by extension, the AFS) were produced by a
real-world biological process (demographic history) which is hidden but which
you want to learn about. Prior bioinformatic studies estimated that the
recombination and mutation rates of this population are both `1e-8` (just like
in humans).**

**Now you want to use this data to estimate the population's long-term $N_e$
which is, of course, unknown (you only have the observed AFS). Suppose that the
only thing known about the population size from some other hypothetical evidence
that this $N_e$ was somewhere between 1000 and 30000.**

($N_e$ is just an example here---in practice, we're typically interested in
other parameters as well (admixture rate, admixture time, split times, etc.),
but the idea remains the same: we computed summaries of the empirical data which
were shaped by those hidden parameters and we need to estimate them.)

Simulations can be a great tool to estimate the most likely value of such an
unknown parameters. **In this exercise, you're going to simulate a large number
of AFS vectors (each resulting from a different assumed $N_e$ value) and then
pick just those $N_e$ values (or just one $N_e$ value) which produced a
simulated AFS closest to the observed AFS.** This is the core idea behind
simulation-based inference and applies to many other situations and modeling
contexts.

To make things manageable, let's decompose the problem into a sequence of steps.











## Part 1: A self-contained data-generating _slendr_ function

**Create a new script `inference_afs.R`. In this script, program a function
called `simulate_afs()`, which will take `Ne` as its only parameter and will
contain a single-population _slendr_ demographic model. In this function, use
`ts_afs()` to compute (and return) the [AFS
vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allele_frequency_spectrum) on a sample of
10 individuals in the tree sequence produced by this model. When you return the
AFS vector from this function, make sure to drop the first and last elements
(with something like `afs[-c(1, 21)]`). Test this function on a couple of `Ne`
values of your choosing, but staying between `Ne = 1000` and `Ne = 30000` and
plot them to observe how (and why) do they differ based on `Ne` parameter you
used in each respective simulation. If you want more information about AFS, see
the help page under `?ts_afs`.**

**Hint:** If you need help, take a look at the exercise chapter which introduced
the concepts of _slendr_ model functions generating some statistics, or feel
free to start building your `inference_afs.R` solution based on the following
"template" (just fill in missing relevant bits of _slendr_ code that you should
be already familiar with).

::: {.aside}

**Note:** If you want to know why I asked you to drop the first and last element
of the `ts_afs()` output (for instance with something like `afs[-c(1, 20)]`),
it's due to technical reasons related to how the underlying _tskit_ module
operates. You don't have to worry about that here, but you can read
[this](https://tskit.dev/tutorials/analysing_tree_sequences.html#sec-tutorial-afs-zeroth-entry)
for more detail.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the "template"

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(slendr)
init_env()

simulate_afs <- function(Ne) {
  # In here you should write code which will:
  #   1. create one population with a given Ne (provided as a function argument)
  #   2. compile the model (either forward-time or backward-time, doesn't matter)
  #   3. simulate a tree sequence
  #   4. select a subset of 10 individuals (you could also schedule ther recording)
  #   5. compute AFS vector from those 10 individuals using `ts_afs()`
  
  # `result` is a variable with your 10-sample AFS vector (we remove the
  # first and last element because it's not meaningful for our example)
  return(result[-c(1, 21)]) 
}

# test the function on a few example runs
afs1k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 1000)
plot(afs1k, type ="o")

afs7k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 7000)
plot(afs7k, type ="o")
```

:::


When used in R, your custom function should work like this (the simulation
is stochastic, so your numbers will be different, of course):

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(slendr)
init_env()

simulate_afs <- function(Ne) {
  # create a slendr model with a single population of size Ne = N
  pop <- population("pop", N = Ne, time = 1000)
  model <- compile_model(pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(pop, Ne))

  # simulate a tree sequence
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  # get the names of the 10 individuals in the tree sequence
  samples <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)

  # compute the AFS vector
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(samples))

  # return the AFS (without the first and last element)
  afs[-c(1, 21)]
}
```

**In summary, your function should give you a vector of singletons, doubletons,
etc., all the way to the number of fixed mutations in our sample of 10
individuals, looking something like this:**

```{r}
simulate_afs(Ne = 1000)
```

<!-- You can visualize this AFS with a simple base R `plot()` function (just for fun, -->
<!-- I'm also plotting the AFS expected from this model [given by a mathematical -->
<!-- formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allele_frequency_spectrum#Calculation), -->
<!-- but you can ignore this, it's just a bonus to further validate the simulation -->
<!-- result): -->

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false
#| code-fold: true
# plot the simulated AFS
plot(simulate_afs(Ne = 1000), type = "o", col = "darkgreen", xlab = "allele frequency", ylab = "count")

# plot the mathematical expectation for the AFS
math_afs <- function(Ne) {
  # compute the expected theta parameter ...
  theta <- 4 * 1e-8 * Ne * 10e6
  # ... and the expected AFS given this theta
  n <- 20 - 1# a sample of 10 diploid individuals means 20 chromosomes
  theta * 1 / 1:n
}
lines(math_afs(Ne = 1000), type = "o", col = "darkblue")

# plot the legend for both AFS vectors
legend("topright", legend = c("simulated AFS", "theoretical AFS"), fill = c("darkgreen", "darkblue"))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

The point of the exercise is for you to force yourself to push through the
frustration. These case studies were designed to put you in a situation in which
you have to address a research problem without a known solution and let you
practice this in a safe environment. Please, only take a look at the solution if
you're either done with your own code, or if you want to compare your solution
to mine:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Here's the complete script `inference_afs.R` so far:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

simulate_afs <- function(Ne) {
  # create a slendr model with a single population of size Ne = N
  pop <- population("pop", N = Ne, time = 1000)
  model <- compile_model(pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

  schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(pop, 10))

  # simulate a tree sequence
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  # get the names of the 10 individuals in the tree sequence
  samples <- ts_names(ts)

  # compute the AFS vector
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(samples))

  # return the AFS (without the first and last element)
  return(afs[-c(1, length(afs))])
}
```

Our function is supposed to produce an AFS vector of counts of alleles observed
at a given frequency in the population sample. Let's verify that our custom
function works correctly by simulating an AFS vector for Ne = 1k, 10k, and 30k:

```{r}
afs_1k <- simulate_afs(1000)
afs_10k <- simulate_afs(10000)
afs_30k <- simulate_afs(30000)
```

Here's one of those vectors. We can see that the function does, indeed, produce
a result of the correct format:

```{r}
afs_1k
```

To see the results of this function in a clearer context, let's visualize
the vectors in the same plot:

```{r}
plot(afs_30k, type = "o", main = "AFS, Ne = 30000", col = "cyan", ylim = c(0, max(afs_30k)))
lines(afs_10k, type = "o", main = "AFS, Ne = 10000", col = "purple")
lines(afs_1k, type = "o", main = "AFS, Ne = 1000", col = "blue")
legend("topright", legend = c("Ne = 1k", "Ne = 10k", "Ne = 30k"),
       fill = c("blue", "purple", "cyan"))
```

:::

:::











## Part 2: Matching simulated AFS against empirical AFS

```{r}
#| output: false
#| echo: false
set.seed(42)
TRUE_NE <- 6543

pop <- population("pop", N = TRUE_NE, time = 100000)
model <- compile_model(pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(pop, 10))

# simulate a tree sequence
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

# get the names of the 10 individuals in the tree sequence
samples <- ts_names(ts)

afs_observed_ <- ts_afs(ts, list(samples))[c(-1, -21)]
dput(afs_observed_)
```

**This is the empirical AFS you computed from the 10 sequenced genomes of your
individuals of interest (perhaps with software like PLINK):**

```{r}
afs_observed <- c(2493, 1167, 876, 649, 539, 543, 381, 330, 338, 211,
                  268, 183, 205, 214, 155, 176, 144, 122, 121)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
if (!all(afs_observed_ == afs_observed)) stop("Unexpected mismatch", call. = FALSE)
```


**Now use your _slendr_ function `simulate_afs()` and a few other techniques you
learned throughout this workshop to "guess" the true (but hidden) $N_e$ of your
population of interest, given this observed AFS. Depending on how confident you
feel with coding, there are two possible options:**

- **Option 1** [easy but not rigorous]: Plot AFS vectors simulated for various
$N_e$ values, then try to guess (just by looking at the AFS visualizations)
which one looks closest to the empirical AFS and, therefore, which simulated
$N_e$ is the closest match to the reality. (This is, of course, not how proper
statistical inference is done, but it's a good start if you're just starting
with simulation-based inference.)

- **Option 2** [harder and more rigorous]: Simulate AFS vectors across a grid of
possible `Ne` values depending on your prior information (perhaps using base R
`lapply()` or _purrr_ `map()`), and find the $N_e$ which results in a simulated
AFS which is closest to the observed AFS by computing [Mean squared
error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_squared_error) on the two of them.











::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution to "Option 1"

This is the empirical AFS to which we need to compare our simulated AFS
vectors:

```{r}
afs_observed <- c(2493, 1167, 876, 649, 539, 543, 381, 330, 338, 211,
                  268, 183, 205, 214, 155, 176, 144, 122, 121)
```

We know that the true $N_e$ is supposed to be between 1000 and 30000, so let's
simulate a couple of AFS vectors for different $N_e$ values using our new AFS
simulation function:

```{r}
afs_Ne1k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 1000)
afs_Ne5k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 5000)
afs_Ne6k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 6000)
afs_Ne10k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 10000)
afs_Ne20k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 20000)
afs_Ne30k <- simulate_afs(Ne = 30000)
```

Now let's plot our simulated AFS vectors together with the observed AFS (shown
in black):

```{r}
plot(afs_observed, type = "b", col = "black", lwd = 3,
     xlab = "allele count bin", ylab = "count", ylim = c(0, 13000))
lines(afs_Ne1k, lwd = 2, col = "blue")
lines(afs_Ne5k, lwd = 2, col = "green")
lines(afs_Ne6k, lwd = 2, col = "pink")
lines(afs_Ne10k, lwd = 2, col = "purple")
lines(afs_Ne20k, lwd = 2, col = "orange")
lines(afs_Ne30k, lwd = 2, col = "cyan")
legend("topright",
       legend = c("observed AFS", "Ne = 1000", "Ne = 5000",
                  "Ne = 6000", "Ne = 10000", "Ne = 20000", "Ne = 30000"),
       fill = c("black", "blue", "green", "pink", "purple", "orange", "cyan"))
```

From the figure, we can see that the black line (empirical AFS) seems to be
closest to the simulated $N_e$ = 6000.

And indeed, I can now reveal that the true $N_e$ of our population of interest
was `{r} TRUE_NE`. Not a bad result for such a simple inference pipeline!

---

Having done the "Option 1" solution, now consider taking a stab at the "Option
2". It's not that much harder, actually, and you've already practiced everything
you need to solve this. You've got this!

:::











::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution to "Option 2"

This is the empirical AFS to which we need to compare our simulated AFS
vectors:

```{r}
afs_observed <- c(2493, 1167, 876, 649, 539, 543, 381, 330, 338, 211,
                  268, 183, 205, 214, 155, 176, 144, 122, 121)
```

We know that the true $N_e$ is supposed to be between 1000 and 30000. Let's
generate a regular grid of potential $N_e$ values for which we want to simulate
AFS vectors:

```{r}
Ne_grid <- seq(from = 1000, to = 30000, by = 500)
Ne_grid
```

With the parameter grid `Ne_grid` set up, let's simulate an AFS from each $N_e$
model (we simply loop over the grid using a parallel version of `lapply()` to
speed things up, but plain `lapply()` or `map()` would work too):

```{r}
library(parallel)

afs_grid <- mclapply(Ne_grid, simulate_afs, mc.cores = detectCores() - 1)
names(afs_grid) <- Ne_grid
```

Here's an example of the first five simulated AFS vectors, just to demonstrate
what the output of the grid simulations looks like. As you can see, we get a
list of numerical vectors, one element of the list corresponding to one AFS (and
indexed by the corresponding `Ne`):

```{r}
afs_grid[1:5]
```

To get a better idea of the grid simulations, let's visualize the observed AFS
(in black) and overlay the simulated AFS vectors on top of it (in gray):

```{r}
# plot the observed AFS in black
plot(afs_observed, type = "b", col = "black", lwd = 3, xlab = "allele count bin", ylab = "count")

# then loop over the list with simulated AFS, overlaying them onto the plot
for (i in seq_along(Ne_grid)) {
  lines(afs_grid[[i]], lwd = 0.5)
}

# add a legend too
legend("topright", legend = c("observed AFS", "simulated AFS"), fill = c("black", "gray"))
```

Instead of just eyeballing the closest AFS like we do in "Option 1" (which is
impossible to do here anyway because of how many AFS vectors we simulated), we
want to compute the [mean squared
error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_squared_error) of the AFS produced by
each $N_e$ value across the grid:

```{r}
# loop over simulated AFS vectors and compute the MSE from the observed AFS for each
error_grid <- sapply(afs_grid, function(afs_simulated) {
  sum((afs_simulated - afs_observed)^2) / length(afs_simulated)
})
```

Let's visualize the error of each simulated AFS and highlight the one which was
closest to the empirical AFS:

```{r}
plot(Ne_grid, error_grid, ylab = "error")

abline(v = Ne_grid[which.min(error_grid)], col = "red")

legend("topright", legend = paste("minimum error Ne =", Ne_grid[which.min(error_grid)]), fill = "red")
```

Plot the AFS again, but this time highlight the AFS which is the most
statistically likely (i.e. the one which gave the lowest MSE value):

```{r}
# plot the observed AFS again
plot(afs_observed, type = "b", col = "black", lwd = 3, xlab = "allele count bin", ylab = "count")

# loop over each simulated AFS...
for (i in seq_along(Ne_grid)) {
  # ... and assign a red color to the one which was the closest based on
  # the computed error from the observed AFS
  color <- if (i == which.min(error_grid)) "red" else "gray"
  width <- if (i == which.min(error_grid)) 2 else 0.75

  lines(afs_grid[[i]], lwd = width, col = color)
}

legend("topright", legend = c("observed AFS", paste("best fitting Ne =", Ne_grid[which.min(error_grid)])),
       fill = c("black", "red"))
```

The true $N_e$ was `{r} TRUE_NE`, which fits our inference result very well!

:::





---





Congratulations, you now know how to infer parameters of evolutionary models
using simulations! What you just did is really very similar to how
simulation-based inference is done in practice (even with methods such as ABC).
Hopefully you now also see how easy _slendr_ makes it to do this process.

As mentioned in the introduction, this kind of approach can be used to infer all
sorts of demographic parameters using simulation-based inference, even using
other summary statistics that you've also learned to compute ($f$-statistics,
nucleotide diversity, IBD data, etc.).
